passage: The lights went out just as the guests arrived, so Dadi lit two lamps in the hall. Lavanya's mother lifted one toward the shelf of trophies won by Lavanya's older brother Abhinav. “Third one this year!” Uncles clapped Abhinav's shoulder. Lavanya's painting of the neem tree, which she had worked on for a week, leaned unnoticed against the wall behind them. She refilled the water jug, then straightened cushions no one had asked her to straighten. Nobody looked her way. Only Dada, sitting near the door, asked, “And what's that behind the shelf?” “Nothing,” Lavanya said, and carried the painting to her room.

qa.q: How many cricket trophies had Abhinav won this year?
qa.a: The mother said it was the third one this year.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya say “Nothing” when Dada asked about the painting?
qa.a: Lavanya seems to feel invisible and does not expect praise, so she brushes the question off even though she worked on the painting for a week.

qa.q: What could the adults do at the next gathering so both children feel seen?
qa.a: They could look at Lavanya's work as warmly as at Abhinav's trophies and ask her about it directly.

qa.q: What might Dada have noticed that the others missed?
qa.a: Dada noticed the painting leaning behind the shelf and asked about it, which suggests he saw Lavanya's quiet effort when the guests did not.

grounding: A child compared with a sibling feels invisible, works quietly for approval and withdraws when nobody looks.

passage: At the colony's Diwali get-together, neighbours crowded round the snack table. “Anjali topped the class again,” the woman from flat 4B told everyone, and Anjali's father beamed. “And Gurpreet?” someone asked. “Oh, he's trying,” said Gurpreet's mother, and people laughed kindly. Gurpreet drifted to the edge of the lawn where the children were lighting sparklers and stood holding a pencil torch nobody needed. Lately he had stopped putting his hand up in class. His sister Anjali glanced across at him. A neighbour, Mr Rao, the retired watchmaker, crouched down. “I hear you fixed the lift buzzer,” he said. Gurpreet shrugged, but stayed standing next to him.

qa.q: Who crouched down beside Gurpreet?
qa.a: Mr Rao, the retired watchmaker, crouched down beside him.

qa.q: What might Gurpreet be feeling as he stands at the edge of the lawn?
qa.a: Gurpreet seems to feel invisible and a little ashamed beside Anjali's praise. The unneeded torch and the hand no longer raised in class suggest he is withdrawing.

qa.q: What small step could the adults take to show Gurpreet he is seen for himself?
qa.a: They could ask about what he has actually done, like fixing the lift buzzer, instead of asking how he compares with Anjali.

qa.q: What might Anjali be feeling as she glances at Gurpreet?
qa.a: Anjali may feel awkward that the praise for her is landing hard on her brother, though the passage only shows her glancing across.

grounding: A boy compared unfavourably with his sister feels quietly invisible and withdraws, and one neighbour sees him.

passage: The school results came on the day of a bus strike, and Papa was stuck at the depot, so Amma went to both parent meetings alone, one after another. Vijay's teacher said he had topped Class 7. Jagdish's teacher said he had improved in every subject. On the way home, Amma bought one box of sweets and phoned everyone: 'Vijay topped!' Jagdish walked a step behind, carrying both school bags. At home, Dadi hugged Vijay and asked Jagdish, 'Why can't you be like your bhaiya?' Jagdish went up to the roof and practised sums till dark. When Papa finally arrived, Jagdish showed him the report card first, and waited.

qa.q: What did Jagdish's teacher say about him?
qa.a: That he had improved in every subject.

qa.q: What was Jagdish probably feeling as he walked a step behind Amma?
qa.a: He likely felt invisible and hurt, since his improvement went unmentioned while Amma phoned everyone about Vijay.

qa.q: What small step could Amma or Dadi take to make Jagdish feel seen?
qa.a: Tell the family about Jagdish's improvement too, and stop comparing him with his bhaiya.

qa.q: How might Vijay experience the same day?
qa.a: Vijay gets hugs and phone calls, so he probably feels proud, and may not even notice his brother carrying both bags behind.

grounding: A child compared unfavourably with a brother feels unseen and works harder for approval, on a hectic results day.

passage: At the Onam lunch in their Kochi flat, the relatives crowded around Anju chechi's dance photos on the phone. 'She'll be on stage in big halls one day,' said Uncle George. Jomon had made the pookalam at the door himself, petal by petal, since six in the morning. Nobody mentioned it. When an aunt asked, 'And Jomon, still weak in maths?' everyone laughed. Jomon went quiet and slipped out to the stairwell. His friend Imran from the next flat found him there. 'That pookalam is the best in the building,' Imran said. Jomon shrugged, but he didn't go back in until the guests had left.

qa.q: What had Jomon made at the door?
qa.a: The pookalam, petal by petal, since six in the morning.

qa.q: Why did Jomon slip out to the stairwell?
qa.a: He felt invisible and embarrassed: his pookalam went unnoticed while Anju chechi's photos were praised, and then everyone laughed about his maths.

qa.q: How could a parent at the lunch have supported Jomon?
qa.a: Point out that Jomon made the pookalam, praise the effort, and stop the maths joke instead of joining the laughter.

qa.q: How does Imran see the situation?
qa.a: Imran notices what the family missed and values Jomon's work, trying to cheer him by calling the pookalam the best in the building.

grounding: A child overshadowed by an older sister at a family gathering feels invisible and withdraws.

passage:
'Gopika got ninety-eight in science!' Mummy announced at dinner.
'That's my girl,' Papa said. 'Siddharth, what about your test?'
'Didn't get it back,' Siddharth muttered.
'You got it back on Tuesday. I saw it in your bag,' said Gopika.
'Why were you in my bag?'
'Siddharth, don't shout at your didi,' Mummy said. 'Why can't you be a bit more like her?'
Siddharth pushed his plate away. 'Because I'm not her. Nobody even asked about my football match.'
There was a pause. Nani, who had been quiet, put down her spoon. 'I asked. He scored a goal. He told me on the phone.'
Papa looked at Siddharth. 'You scored?'
'Doesn't matter,' Siddharth said, but he stayed at the table.

qa.q: What did Gopika get in science?
qa.a: Ninety-eight.

qa.q: What does Siddharth pushing his plate away suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels angry and overlooked after being compared with his didi again, and hurt that nobody asked about his match.

qa.q: What could Mummy and Papa try next time at dinner?
qa.a: Ask each child about their own day, like Siddharth's football match, and drop the 'be more like her' comparison.

qa.q: How might Nani see this dinner?
qa.a: Nani has noticed what the parents missed, Siddharth's goal, and speaks up so that he is seen.

grounding: A boy compared with his sister at dinner feels invisible and pushes back, until a grandmother points out what he did.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage:
I'm Nirmala. My didi, Reena, is in Class 9 and has a whole shelf of trophies. When relatives visit, Amma shows them the shelf. Then someone asks, "And Nirmala?" and Amma says, "She's the quiet one."
Last month I got a gold star for my story about our cat. I left it on the dining table all evening. Nobody saw it under the newspaper. So I started staying up doing extra sums, hoping for a trophy of my own. Some days I think I'll just stop trying.
Last Sunday, Reena didi found my story in my bag. She read it twice, laughed at the cat part and pinned it on the fridge. I pretended I didn't care. I checked it was still there five times.

qa.q: What did Nirmala get a gold star for?
qa.a: A story about the family cat.

qa.q: How did Nirmala feel when nobody noticed the gold star?
qa.a: Nirmala felt invisible and disappointed, so much that she sometimes wants to stop trying.

qa.q: What small thing could Amma do to help Nirmala feel seen?
qa.a: Ask about Nirmala's own work, like the cat story, and show it to relatives instead of only the trophy shelf.

qa.q: Why might Reena have pinned the story on the fridge?
qa.a: Reena seemed to enjoy the story and may have sensed her sister felt overlooked, wanting it to be seen 🤍

grounding: Shows a younger child compared with a high-achieving sister, feeling quietly invisible and swinging between working harder and giving up.
